title: United Airlines Flight 173: fuel-state monitoring, fixation under landing-gear anomaly, and CRM correction surface
summary: United 173 is encoded as a flight-deck state and CRM precursor case: the aircraft remained airborne while the crew addressed a landing-gear indication problem, but fuel-state monitoring, communication, and command-gradient dynamics failed to convert a deteriorating state into timely landing action.

status_history.note: Added as rev0027 flight-deck state / CRM rail lane record.

claims.claim: The NTSB investigation page identifies United Airlines Flight 173 as a December 28, 1978 accident near Portland after the aircraft remained at low altitude for about one hour while the crew coped with a landing-gear malfunction and prepared for emergency landing, with eight passengers, the flight engineer, and a flight attendant killed and serious injuries to 21 passengers and two crew members.
what_would_change_status: A second-pass source review materially revises the extraction, narrows its scope, or adds a stronger primary source.

claims.claim: The NTSB probable-cause summary emphasizes the captain’s failure to monitor fuel state and respond to crew advisories, and identifies the other flightcrew members’ failure to communicate fuel-criticality or comprehend the captain’s attention as contributing factors.
what_would_change_status: A second-pass source review materially revises the extraction, narrows its scope, or adds a stronger primary source.

claims.claim: The FAA Lessons Learned module treats the cockpit hierarchy and communication pattern as ineffective crew-resource management, including the second officer’s failure to assert fuel criticality and the captain’s apparent lack of awareness after engine flameouts.
what_would_change_status: A second-pass source review materially revises the extraction, narrows its scope, or adds a stronger primary source.

claims.claim: The same FAA module records recommendations including flight crew training and uses the case to emphasize participative/collaborative cockpit processes that allow crew members to speak up.
what_would_change_status: A second-pass source review materially revises the extraction, narrows its scope, or adds a stronger primary source.

type_payload.system: Douglas DC-8 flight crew / fuel state / landing-gear indication and emergency-preparation context
sequence_of_events: Landing-gear indication problem absorbed attention; crew delayed landing while troubleshooting/preparing emergency; fuel state degraded; engine flameouts occurred; aircraft crashed short of runway.
type_payload.proximate_cause: fuel exhaustion after delayed landing under landing-gear troubleshooting context
contributing_factors: captain attention/fixation and fuel-state monitoring failure
crew advisories did not become decisive shared state
emergency-preparation workload and abnormal situation management
latent_conditions: pre-modern CRM training and cockpit hierarchy norms
lessons later encoded into CRM and FAA lessons-learned surfaces

handling_notes: Aviation records must preserve the dignity of passengers, crew, families, responders, and survivors.
Do not flatten human-factors findings into pilot blame; separate physical system state, displayed state, automation mode, training, procedures, supervision, fatigue, and investigation/legal status.
This is historical/evidentiary infrastructure, not operational flight-safety guidance or legal advice.

unknowns: Full NTSB report and recommendation closure were not re-extracted in this pass; NTSB landing-page summary and FAA module were used for bounded claims.
The record does not adjudicate individual culpability or legal history.
